summary.text: A pulsar is a highly magnetized, rotating neutron star that sends beams of electromagnetic radiation out of its magnetic poles.
The radiation is seen only when a beam points toward Earth, the way a lighthouse is seen only when its light points toward an observer.
Because neutron stars have short, regular rotational periods, pulses arrive at very precise intervals, which makes pulsars very useful tools for astronomers.

facts.label: First found
facts.value: By Jocelyn Bell, in data recorded August 6, 1967

facts.label: First exoplanets
facts.value: Found in 1992 around pulsar PSR B1257+12

facts.label: Fast spinner
facts.value: PSR B1937+21 rotates about every 1.6 milliseconds

items.prompt: A pulsar's beams sweep steadily through space, yet telescopes see it blink on and off. Why?

options.label: The star itself switches its energy output on and off
We only catch a beam when it points our way
Dust clouds keep passing in front of it
A companion star keeps blocking its light

items.explain: The radiation is observed only when a beam points toward Earth, like a lighthouse, which produces the pulsed appearance.

items.prompt: Jocelyn Bell's supervisor first dismissed her signals as radio interference. What soon ruled that out?

options.label: A second telescope abroad heard nothing at all
They were louder at night than during the day
They matched the pattern of known satellites
They always came from the same position on the sky

items.explain: Because the signals always appeared at the same declination and right ascension, a terrestrial source was ruled out.

items.prompt: What finally killed the idea that the first pulsar's signals were an alien message?

options.label: Finding another pulsing source in a different part of the sky
The pulses stopped once the telescope was repaired
A radio engineer traced them to a nearby factory
The pulses turned out to be too irregular for a message

items.explain: Bell's discovery of a second pulsar quashed the speculation, and the LGM hypothesis was abandoned once a second source appeared elsewhere in the sky.

items.prompt: In 1974 a pulsar was found orbiting another neutron star every eight hours. What did watching it show?

options.label: Its pulses were bent by passing gravitational waves
It was falling into a nearby black hole
Its orbit kept contracting, as relativity predicted for gravitational waves
Its beam split in two, as relativity predicted

items.explain: General relativity predicts the system should radiate gravitational waves and lose orbital energy; observations confirmed this, giving the first evidence for gravitational waves.

items.prompt: The Crab Pulsar blinks about thirty times a second. Why did that help settle what pulsars are?

options.label: It proved pulsars are heavy stars that swell and shrink
That rate was too quick for other models but fit a rotating neutron star
It showed the pulses come from a companion eclipsing the star
It showed pulsars send pulses only when they are very young

items.explain: The 33-millisecond period was too short to be consistent with other proposed emission models, and its discovery confirmed the rotating neutron star model.

items.prompt: Why would an astronomer treat a pulsar like a clock?

options.label: Its pulses arrive at very precise, evenly spaced intervals
Its brightness cycles daily, in step with Earth's day
Its light stays the same colour from year to year
It always stays at the same distance from Earth

items.explain: Neutron stars have short, regular rotational periods, giving a very precise interval between pulses; some pulsars even beat atomic clocks.

paragraphs.heading: A cosmic lighthouse
paragraphs.text: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star with a very strong magnetic field that sends out beams of radiation from its magnetic poles. We only see a beam when it points at Earth, the way a lighthouse is seen only when its light faces you, and that is why it seems to pulse. Neutron stars spin with short, regular periods, so the pulses arrive at very precise intervals, from milliseconds to seconds apart.

paragraphs.heading: An odd signal
paragraphs.text: Jocelyn Bell first spotted signals from a pulsar in data recorded on August 6, 1967, by a new radio telescope she had helped build. Her supervisor, Antony Hewish, first took it for radio interference. But the signal always came from the same spot in the sky, which ruled out a source on Earth. On November 28, 1967, the two resolved it into pulses evenly spaced every 1.337 seconds, and they nicknamed it LGM-1, for little green men.

paragraphs.heading: Not aliens after all
paragraphs.text: On December 21, Bell found a second pulsar in a different part of the sky, and the idea that the signals came from aliens was dropped. The first pulsar is now known by several names, including PSR B1919+21. It gives off radio waves, but pulsars have since been found that shine in visible light, X-rays and gamma rays.

paragraphs.heading: Explaining the pulses
paragraphs.text: In 1967, shortly before the discovery, Franco Pacini suggested that a spinning neutron star with a magnetic field would give off radiation. After the first pulsar was found, Thomas Gold independently made a similar proposal and argued that it could explain the pulses. Lovelace and colleagues then found that the pulsar in the Crab Nebula has a period of about 33 ms. That was too short for the other proposed models, so it confirmed the spinning neutron star picture.

paragraphs.heading: A prize and a controversy
paragraphs.text: In 1974 Hewish and Martin Ryle became the first astronomers to win the Nobel Prize in Physics. Bell, who made the first discovery while she was Hewish's PhD student, was not included, and this caused a lot of controversy. Bell herself says she feels no bitterness and supports the committee's decision.

paragraphs.heading: Clocks in the sky
paragraphs.text: Their very regular pulses make pulsars useful tools. In 1974 Joseph Hooton Taylor, Jr. and Russell Hulse found the first pulsar in a binary system, PSR B1913+16, which circles another neutron star every eight hours. General relativity predicts that such a pair should lose energy as gravitational radiation, so its orbit keeps shrinking, and observations confirmed this, giving the first evidence of gravitational waves. Pulsars also hosted the first planets found outside our Solar System, discovered in 1992 around PSR B1257+12.

paragraphs.heading: Millisecond pulsars
paragraphs.text: In 1982 a group led by Don Backer found PSR B1937+21, which turns once in about 1.6 milliseconds. Its magnetic field turned out to be much weaker than that of ordinary pulsars. More finds showed that a new class had been found, the millisecond pulsars, which are thought to be the end product of X-ray binaries.
